title: Render to Caesar (Mark 11:27–12:17)
hook: a coin with Caesar's image; what bears God's image belongs to God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fig tree and the temple: all leaves, no fruit, and a lesson that ended in forgiveness. Your line was forgive, then pray. What did you set down first? Today, Jesus is back in the Temple, and they've come to trap him. Day two hundred twenty-two.

You know the question that has no safe answer. The one at a family dinner that's really a trap: whichever way you answer, somebody's furious. Jesus walks the Temple courts, and the questions start. By what authority do you do these things? He answers with a question of his own, and tells a story about tenants who kill the owner's son. Then a group arrives with the perfect trap. Some are Pharisees. Some are supporters of Herod. They flatter him first. Then they ask: should we pay taxes to Caesar, or not?
screen: `A QUESTION WITH NO SAFE ANSWER.` → `BY WHAT AUTHORITY?` → `PAY TAXES TO CAESAR, OR NOT?`

segments.voice: First, the trap. If he says yes, pay, he sides with Rome, the occupier, and the crowd turns on him. If he says no, don't pay, he's a rebel, and Rome has a cross for rebels. There's no safe answer. Second, the coin. He says, bring me a penny, let me see it. The coin is a Roman denarius, the tax coin. And he asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whose is this image and inscription?" They say: Caesar's. The emperor's face is on it, and around the edge, words calling him the son of a god. Notice: he has to ask them for one. They're the ones carrying Caesar's coin into the Temple. Third, the answer: render "to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Mark says they marveled at him. It's not a dodge. It's an answer with a hook in it. The coin has Caesar's image, so it belongs to him; give it back. Then what has God's image on it? Every Jewish listener knew Genesis. In the Douay-Rheims: "And God created man to his own image: to the image of God he created him." Early Christian writers loved this: the coin carries Caesar's face, and you carry God's. Fourth, what this means for Catholics now. The Church teaches that Christians owe real duties to their country: pay taxes, vote, serve the common good. But the state doesn't own the whole person. The deepest part, the image, belongs to God. So the line both honors earthly duty and sets a limit on it. Your wallet can go to Caesar. You can't.
screen: `A TRAP WITH NO SAFE ANSWER.` · `WHOSE IMAGE IS ON THE COIN?` · `GIVE CAESAR HIS COIN.` · `YOU CARRY GOD'S IMAGE.` · then, large: `AND TO GOD THE THINGS THAT ARE GOD'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at your own face in a mirror. If there's one nearby, or your phone's camera, look now. If not, picture your face. Resist the usual checklist: hair, skin, tired eyes. Just look, the way you'd look at a coin to see whose image it bears. Catholics say that face was made in the image of God. Stay with that for a while. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let yourself be looked at kindly, even by yourself. The bell holds the time.
Render to Caesar. Give back to Caesar the coin with his face on it, and to God what bears God's image. Today's word.
Your line: you bear his image. Today, when you see a face, a stranger's, an annoying one, your own, remember whose image it's said to carry. Day two hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church teaches that citizens have duties to the state, such as paying taxes and voting, and that every human being is made in the image of God, which grounds its teaching on human dignity.

original.note: Greek: image, the word on the coin, and the word the Greek Bible uses for the image of God in Genesis. icon comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: church and state, separated.
what it means: give the coin back to the one whose face is on it, and give yourself to the one whose image you bear.
what a scholar hears: eikōn, the same word as the Greek Genesis 1:27; a denarius of Tiberius, 'son of the divine Augustus'.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 12:16, 12:17 and Genesis 1:27 given from memory; confirm.

The tribute coin is usually identified as a denarius of Tiberius with the inscription 'Ti. Caesar Divi Aug. F. Augustus' (Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus); the script says 'words calling him the son of a god'. Confirm.
'Early Christian writers loved this' (image-on-coin / image-of-God reading; e.g. Tertullian, Against Marcion 4.38; Augustine): confirm attribution before naming anyone.
The Greek Old Testament uses eikōn at Genesis 1:27: confirm.
Catholic teaching on civic duty (CCC 2238–2240) paraphrased: confirm references.
